extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry; literary critics and readers learning practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close-reading and evaluating lyric and metrical poetry, focusing on the interaction of sound, metre, sense, imagery, and reader response. Emphasises common reading errors (mechanical metre-reading, irrelevant associations, stock responses) and practices to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm as projected from sense and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic rhythm that we admire is often "projected" — a rhythm of the mental activity through which we apprehend not only the sound of the words but their sense and feeling, rather than being wholly inherent in the physical sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that the kymograph/physical recording of sound will distinguish 'good' from 'bad' poetry. The apparent superiority of a poem's sound can be a reflection of the adjustment of our feelings invoked by its sense. Examine how sense and feeling contribute to perceived rhythm rather than treating sound as autonomous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound is important but must be judged with sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual sounds (the inherent rhythm) are a very important contributing factor but cannot be judged apart from the sense and feeling of the words out of which they are composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sounds as the 'skeleton' upon which the reader 'casts flesh and clothing.' If the skeleton (sounds/metre) is badly mismatched to sense and feeling, no amount of reader goodwill will make the verse succeed. Test by altering rhythm while preserving vocabulary/syntax to see effects (example: forced metre turning a noble line into comic-opera patter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical pattern is a convenience, not a compulsory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The pattern (metre) 'indicates the general movement of the rhythm' and provides a model and point of orientation, but it has no compulsory powers and verses are under no obligation to conform to any standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical, pattern-blind scanning and equally avoid rejecting poems for irregularity alone. Use the pattern as a support and central line from which meaningful variations derive; resist 'cruel forcing' of syllables into a mould they were not meant to fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning influences perceived rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived/ascribed rhythm is strongly influenced by our apprehension of meaning: phrases with similar inherent sounds may be scanned the same prosodically yet read differently because of meaning (e.g., 'Deep into a gloomy grot' vs 'Peep into a roomy cot').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rhythm, consider semantic and syntactic differences that shape prosodic movement. Experiments with nonsense syllables show that without meaning the supposed independent aesthetic virtue of mere sound is greatly diminished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and meaning must cooperate (chief secret of Style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The close co-operation of the form with the meaning — each modifying the other — is generally the chief secret of Style in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by how their formal elements (metre, cadence, sound-patterns) interact with their sense and feeling. Look for purposeful distortions of metre by sense and note whether such departures form a coherent whole rather than accidental dissonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing judgment on idiosyncratic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid, precise images arising for a particular reader may owe much to sources outside the poet's control and may be irrelevant to the poem's meaning; the merit of a poem is not established simply because it 'calls up a beautiful picture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between imagery that genuinely embodies the poem's meaning and imagery that is a personal or accidental reaction. Give weight to the general character and feeling of imagery rather than to incidental pictorial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use associations and comparisons only when deeply grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations with other poems or ideas are relevant only if the link is deep and rooted in the inner nature and structure of the works; superficial resemblances (title, a phrase, or shared theme/metrical class) prove nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ comparisons chiefly as tools to prompt closer reading. Avoid classifying poems by external categories (themes, metres) and then assuming poems in the same class 'must be alike.' Trace resemblances to their deeper structural or semantic grounds before treating them as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of irrelevant personal memories and stock responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader's personal memories or stereotyped (stock) responses can intrude and make the reading largely a response to the reader's reminiscence rather than to the poem; stock responses are habitual reactions that may be convenient but can be disadvantageous and distort the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow personal memories only if they are genuine and relevant and respect the poem's autonomy. Diagnose stock responses (automatic epithets, conventional emotional reactions, stock rhythms) and attempt to set them aside to see whether more adequate readings develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise energetic, interest-driven interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations are not passive: the most 'attractive' or active interpretation in a reader's mind will be adopted. Every interpretation is motivated by some interest, and prepossessions (desire for approval/condemnation) can seize the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware: check for dominant interests or preconceptions that bias reading. Cultivate the major interest of faithful reading and watchful control to prevent initial desires from dictating judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private slow reading is a better method for discovering form
rubrics_metrics.description: Private reading aloud is recommended as an aid in working out a poem's form; public reading (in the classroom) should be discouraged until the poem has revealed most of its secrets. Readers are more likely to read too fast than too slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer slow, private perusal when the rhythm is not yet clear, to allow interaction of form and meaning. Avoid premature public performance that may mislead others or instill bad habits; be cautious of gramophone/recorded renditions which are often poor and may sentimentalise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect impersonality and native familiarity as signs of stock composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems whose mental movements are extremely familiar and impersonal — where phrasing has no personal twist and could be 'written by a committee' — often consist of stock responses and lack individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate originality and personal character: native familiarity and impersonality may indicate the poem is composed of ready-made responses. Contrast with highly individualized diction (e.g., Donne's sonnet quoted) to appreciate personal character as a virtue.
